Why Most Gastroenterologists Won’t Tell You What’s Actually Happening Inside Your Stomach

Dr. Lena Park is a board-certified gastroenterologist. She’s spent the last six years specializing in GLP-1-related digestive complications — the population most clinicians dismiss with a one-size-fits-all “drink more water, eat more fiber, or just try miralax” recommendation.

In a recent interview, she explained why the standard advice fails for women on Wegovy, Ozempic, and Mounjaro and why a small group of researchers has been quietly developing a natural formula that works on the actual root cause.

Here’s what she told us:

“The problem is that the entire medical playbook for constipation was written before GLP-1 medications existed. Every product in your medicine cabinet — Miralax, Dulcolax, fiber gummies, Smooth Move tea — is designed to act on the colon.”

“But GLP-1 medications don’t slow the colon. They slow the stomach.”

“The stomach loses its rhythm. Food sits there for hours. Sometimes days. It ferments. That’s where the sulfur burps come from. By the time anything reaches the colon — if it reaches at all — it’s already a brick. The colon isn’t the problem. The colon is empty.”

What’s more…

“Every laxative you’ve tried targets the colon, six feet downstream from where the actual problem is. They cannot work. The mechanics make it impossible.”

But that’s not all…

She also explained why the doctors prescribing these medications rarely mention this.

“GLP-1s were approved as appetite suppressants. The slowed gastric motility is listed as a side effect — but it’s a peripheral effect of the drug working systemically, not the mechanism that drives weight loss. Most prescribing physicians focus on the appetite mechanism because that’s what the patient came in for. The stomach effect gets a one-line warning and a Miralax recommendation.”

Dr. Park recently helped review a new natural formula developed specifically for GLP-1-related digestive symptoms — one that works on the stomach instead of the colon, addressing the actual mechanical issue the medication creates.

So you can stop tracking your bowel movements in a spreadsheet. Stop wearing baggy clothes by 2 PM. Stop dreading dinner with your husband.

Dr. Park Tells It As It Is:

“For years, women on these medications have been quietly told to either tolerate the digestive symptoms or lower their dose.”

“And lowering the dose isn’t an option for most of them. They’ve finally found something that silences the food noise. They’re losing weight for the first time in twenty years. They’re not going off the medication. So they suffer in silence.”

The reason why?

“Because the system is set up to address the appetite side, not the gastric side. Until something works on the actual mechanical problem, you’re just cycling through laxatives that target an organ that isn’t the issue.”

“A patient who tolerates the side effects in silence is a successful case.”

— Dr. Lena Park

The Mechanism Almost Every GLP-1 Constipation Treatment Has Missed

The slowed gastric motility caused by GLP-1 medications creates three downstream problems simultaneously — and almost every product on the market addresses only one of them, usually the wrong one.

Problem 1
The Stomach Has Stopped Moving Food Through
Standard laxatives don’t touch this. They work in the colon.
↓
Problem 2
Food Sitting in a Stalled Stomach Ferments
Bacteria produce hydrogen sulfide gas — the same compound that gives rotten eggs their smell. This is where the sulfur burps come from. No fiber supplement, probiotic, or laxative addresses this.
↓
Problem 3
Weeks of Stalled Motility Creates Downstream Congestion
Adding bulk fiber to a backed-up system makes it worse. It’s like packing more cars onto a highway where the on-ramp is closed.

A formula that actually addresses GLP-1 constipation has to do all three things at once:

Wake the stomach back up — restore gastric motility without overriding the medication

Neutralize the sulfur gas — disarm the molecule, not mask the smell

Soften the downstream backup — without adding bulk to a jammed system

Until recently, no single product on the market combined all three.
